region: Exact 1492 atlas polygon across the Yucatán Peninsula and adjacent Maya lowlands, interpreted through localized Late Postclassic evidence
researcher: Codex parallel release150-maya-yucateco research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Human History Map civilization index
sources.note: Exact target id, label, dates, circa marker, and generated provenance.

sources.title: Human History Map research coverage registry
sources.note: One observed interval, one border file, missing card state, and unreviewed identity metadata.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 borders
sources.note: Pre-target control, broad maya ownership, and absence of the exact id.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 borders
sources.note: Only exact target feature, decoded polygon, point ownership, and encoded Garifuna seam.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 borders
sources.note: Exact endpoint snapshot, target removal, and return of broad maya ownership.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 borders
sources.note: Post-end control separating later mayas and New Spain assignments from the target interval.

sources.title: UNESCO: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna
sources.note: UNESCO chronology places Garifuna settlement on the Atlantic coast of Central America after eighteenth-century expulsion from Saint Vincent.

sources.title: Library of Congress: The 1562 Map of America
sources.note: Institutional overview locating Columbus first at Guanahani in the Bahamas and early Spanish exploration in Atlantic and Caribbean contexts.

sources.title: INAH: Chultun discovered at Tulum
sources.note: Official excavation report distinguishes rainwater receivers from a chamber interpreted for storage and later ritual use.

sources.title: Usos de la voz 'maya' y reivindicacion identitaria en una carta inedita en lengua maya yucateca del siglo XVI
sources.note: Caroline Cunill, Estudios de Cultura Maya / UNAM. Shows that meaning and usage of the word Maya must be demonstrated in context. Caution: A late-sixteenth-century attestation cannot establish universal 1492 usage.

sources.title: Rural resilience following the collapse of Mayapan
sources.note: Journal of Anthropological Archaeology. Supports continuity and adaptation outside a capital-centered collapse story. Caution: Regional samples still cannot describe every 1492 town.

sources.title: Campeche en la conquista y la colonizacion del mundo maya
sources.note: Arturo Gomez, UNAM Facultad de Filosofia y Letras. Supports the conventional 1502 first-recorded-contact chronology and canoe commerce. Caution: 1502 lies outside the atlas window; canoe origin/identity is reconstructed.

sources.title: Modern Editions of Colonial Spanish and Maya Sources: Linguistics and Manuscript Guide
sources.note: The Newberry Library. Helps identify edition and transmission history before quoting colonial Maya texts. Caution: A guide, not substantive evidence for a 1492 practice.

sources.title: Population movement on the east coast of the Yucatan Peninsula during the Late Postclassic
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Supports mobility and interaction rather than isolated fixed communities. Caution: Bioarchaeological samples are local and cannot assign ethnic identity by themselves.

sources.title: Survival and Revival of Terminal Classic Traditions at Postclassic Mayapan
sources.note: Susan Milbrath and Carlos Peraza Lope, Latin American Antiquity. Shows selective continuity and revival in ceramics, architecture, iconography, and calendrical monuments. Caution: Continuity does not mean an unchanged civilization or direct survival into every 1492 community.

sources.title: Revisiting Mayapan, Mexico's Last Maya Capital
sources.note: Susan Milbrath and Carlos Peraza Lope. Archaeological reassessment of chronology, monuments, and political-religious life. Caution: The phrase last capital must not become last Maya state or end of Maya civilization.

sources.title: The Chronology of Mayapan: New Radiocarbon Evidence
sources.note: Carlos Peraza Lope, Marilyn A. Masson, Timothy S. Hare, and Pedro Candelario Delgado Ku. Essential for preventing false year-level precision in Mayapan's rise and abandonment. Caution: Radiocarbon ranges do not establish a single exact fall date.

sources.title: The Political Geography of the Sixteenth Century Yucatan Maya: Comments and Revisions
sources.note: Anthony P. Andrews. Documents revisions to Roys and supports explicit boundary uncertainty. Caution: Still relies on later colonial evidence.

sources.title: Maya Lords and Lordship: The Formation of Colonial Society in Yucatan, 1350-1600
sources.note: Sergio Quezada, University of Oklahoma Press. Emphasizes interpersonal networks of lordship and their colonial transformation. Caution: Avoid reducing its relational model to neat bounded provinces.

sources.title: Mexico, grandeza y diversidad: territorio maya and the 1517 expedition
sources.note: Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia (INAH). Accessible institutional chronology: no single Maya empire, 1511 shipwreck survivors, 1517 Hernandez de Cordoba landfall. Caution: All events are after 1500; public synthesis compresses contested details.

sources.title: Settlement, Economy, and Society at Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico
sources.note: Marilyn A. Masson, Timothy S. Hare, Carlos Peraza Lope et al., University of Pittsburgh. Detailed site-level data on houselots, middens, domestic economy, and social variation. Caution: Site phase and context must accompany each borrowed detail.

sources.title: Famine foods and food security in the northern Maya lowlands: modern lessons for ancient reconstructions
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Useful against a maize-only diet and for explaining risk-spreading strategies. Caution: Modern plant use does not prove exact pre-contact use without archaeological evidence.

sources.title: Groundwater hydrology of the Yucatan Peninsula
sources.note: Journal of Hydrology. Explains karst aquifer and why cenotes/groundwater structured settlement and water access. Caution: Environmental setting alone does not document household water practice.

sources.title: The Weight of Water: A New Look at Prehispanic Puuc Maya Water Reservoirs
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Supports engineered water storage and the labor/social consequences of stored water. Caution: Puuc water constraints differ from cenote-rich zones; much evidence predates 1492.

sources.title: Interregional interaction in Terminal Classic Yucatan: obsidian and ceramic data from Vista Alegre
sources.note: Latin American Antiquity. Documents interregional coastal exchange and imported materials. Caution: Earlier than target; establishes network history, not 1492 cargo lists.

sources.title: Ancient Maya Commerce: Multidisciplinary Research at Chunchucmil
sources.note: Scott R. Hutson, editor, University Press of Colorado. Methodologically strong evidence for marketplaces, household production, movement, and commerce in northern Yucatan. Caution: Earlier city; use as regional economic background, not direct 1492 description.

sources.title: Origin of the Dresden Maya Codex
sources.note: Saxon State and University Library Dresden (SLUB). Strongest nearby-period manuscript evidence: screenfold production, six scribal hands, calendrical/ritual consultation. Caution: No exact 1492-1500 date or archaeological provenance; the library's 1521 endpoint is a broad convention.

sources.title: Codice Trocortesiano (Madrid Codex)
sources.note: Museo de America, Ministerio de Cultura de Espana. Canonical holding-institution source for a Late Postclassic screenfold with ritual and almanac content. Caution: Fifteenth century is too broad to call any page an exact 1492 sample.

sources.title: Tributos, limosnas y mantas en Yucatan, siglo XVI
sources.note: Sergio Quezada, Ancient Mesoamerica. Shows cloth's importance in colonial tribute and labor systems. Caution: Colonial extraction changed scale and organization; not a direct 1492 labor ledger.

sources.title: Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517-1570
sources.note: Inga Clendinnen, Cambridge University Press. Canonical account of the later, prolonged and contested conquest; documents Montejo's 1527 expedition. Caution: Entirely after the target window.

sources.title: El golfo de Honduras: estrategias geopoliticas y militares de una frontera imperial, siglos XVI-XVIII
sources.note: Fronteras de la Historia / SciELO Mexico. Corroborates the 1502 fourth-voyage canoe encounter and its location outside northern Yucatan. Caution: Outside both the 1492-1500 interval and the principal mapped region.

sources.title: Maya Ethnogenesis
sources.note: Matthew Restall. Core warning against treating Maya as a timeless, uniform ethnic self-name. Caution: A historiographic argument, not proof that no person ever used the word.

sources.title: Maya Ethnogenesis and Group Identity in Yucatan, 1500-1900
sources.note: Matthew Restall and Wolfgang Gabbert, University Press of Colorado. Strongest accessible source for local/community identity and the lack of a consistent umbrella self-name. Caution: Its thesis should be represented as an argument grounded mainly in colonial-language evidence.

sources.title: Catálogo de las Lenguas Indígenas Nacionales: maya
sources.note: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI). Supports modern names including maaya, maaya t'aan, and maayáa and current distribution. Caution: Modern autonyms must not be projected backward as a universal 1492 collective self-name.

sources.title: Living Maya Time
sources.note: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian. Authoritative public-facing resource for living Maya communities and calendar continuity. Caution: Modern practice is not an unchanged survival of a single 1492 norm.

sources.title: Drought and societal change: the environmental context for the emergence of violence at Mayapan
sources.note: Douglas J. Kennett et al., Nature Communications. Integrates climate, chronology, violence, and political instability while also discussing regional resilience. Caution: Climate is one factor in a multicausal history; do not write deterministic collapse.

sources.title: The Political Geography of the Yucatan Maya
sources.note: Ralph L. Roys, Carnegie Institution of Washington. Foundational reconstruction of regional provinces/lordships from colonial records. Caution: Old and revised; its polygons are hypotheses, not surveyed 1492 borders.

sources.title: The Maya World: Yucatec Culture and Society, 1550-1850
sources.note: Matthew Restall. Uses Maya-language documentation to reconstruct colonial towns, households, social relations, and continuity. Caution: Begins half a century after the target window; never cite as direct 1492 observation.

sources.title: Early Maya navigation and maritime connections in Mesoamerica
sources.note: Heather McKillop, Cambridge University Press. Strong synthesis of direct and indirect evidence for canoe travel, fishing, and maritime trade. Caution: Do not assume the 1502 vessel came from a particular Yucatan polity without qualification.

sources.title: Kukulkan's Realm: Urban Life at Ancient Mayapan
sources.note: Marilyn A. Masson and Carlos Peraza Lope, University Press of Colorado. Major synthesis of urban neighborhoods, households, production, exchange, institutions, and inequality. Caution: Mayapan is not the whole peninsula and much evidence predates 1492.

sources.title: Rural houselots and communities in the Mayapan polity
sources.note: University Press of Florida / Florida Scholarship Online. Counterweight to capital-focused evidence; supports rural domestic and community life. Caution: Association with the Mayapan polity may predate the atlas window.

sources.title: Ancient Maya waste management: archaeological evidence and research gaps
sources.note: Estudios de Cultura Maya / UNAM. Best explicit evidence-gap source for human-waste disposal and sanitation research. Caution: Its no-published-evidence conclusion predates the 2022 San Bartolo biomarker study; phrase historically, not absolutely.

sources.title: He Wished It in Vain: Subordination and Resistance among Maya Women in Post-Conquest Yucatan
sources.note: Matthew Restall. Uses Maya-language legal records to recover women's property, agency, and constraints. Caution: Later colonial law and documentation bias; not a pre-contact role checklist.

sources.title: The Ties That Bind: Social Cohesion and the Yucatec Maya Family
sources.note: Matthew Restall, Journal of Family History. Maya-language records illuminate marriage, household, kin, and property relations. Caution: Colonial institutions and demographic shocks altered households.

sources.title: Poor Mayapan: household inequality and house-size evidence
sources.note: Cambridge University Press. Supports discussion of ordinary households and material inequality rather than an elite-only portrait. Caution: Poverty labels are analytical; avoid equating small houses with simple lives.

sources.title: The Social Experience of Childhood in Ancient Mesoamerica
sources.note: Traci Ardren and Scott R. Hutson, editors; Smithsonian Libraries record. Supports treating children as active social participants rather than miniature adults or invisible dependents. Caution: Comparative volume; only Maya/Yucatan chapters can ground local claims.

sources.title: The Maya Calendar System
sources.note: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian. Clear child-facing explanation of interlocking counts without apocalypse myths. Caution: Regional systems and historical use varied.

sources.title: Maya astronomical observations and the agricultural cycle in the Postclassic Madrid Codex
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Evidence for sophisticated observation connecting sky, calendar, ritual, and farming cycles. Caution: Interpretive study of a broadly dated manuscript; avoid exact-year claims.

sources.title: Testimonios visuales de la ninez entre los mayas del Clasico
sources.note: Liminal / CESMECA-UNICACH. Useful methodological source for visibility and interpretation of children. Caution: Images are not transparent photographs of daily routine; not exact-period Yucatan.

sources.title: Effigy censer and figurine production at the Postclassic Maya city of Mayapan
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Links specialized ceramic production to ritual objects and distribution. Caution: Specific workshops and site phase; do not generalize production organization.

sources.title: Animal use at the Postclassic Maya center of Mayapan
sources.note: Quaternary International. Documents food, craft, ritual, and status uses of animals in excavated contexts. Caution: Mayapan predates the target and is not representative of every ecology.

sources.title: Rejolladas and agricultural use at Tahcabo, Yucatan
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Supports nuanced use of karst depressions as productive microenvironments. Caution: Not every rejollada was cultivated identically or in every period.

sources.title: Perfect storm: climate change and ancient Maya response in the Puuc Hills region of Yucatan
sources.note: Antiquity. Detailed archaeological evidence for integrated water systems and environmental risk. Caution: Earlier than target; use as technology background only.

sources.title: The organization of stingless beekeeping (Meliponiculture) at Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico
sources.note: Journal of Anthropological Archaeology. Supports meliponiculture, honey/wax production, exchange, and ritual use. Caution: Context largely predates 1492; later descriptions must be labeled.

sources.title: Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan
sources.note: Diego de Landa; Wayeb hosted edition. Detailed but compromised testimony on calendar, writing, ritual, food, healing, social life, and Spanish violence. Caution: Hostile missionary author, inquisitorial context, written decades later after Landa's 1562 destruction of books; never neutral or exact-period.

sources.title: Maya coastal production, exchange, life style, and population mobility: a view from the port of Xcambo
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Strong regional precedent for salt/coastal production, exchange, mobility, and diet. Caution: Earlier than 1492; use only as regional background, not exact-period proof.

sources.title: Zooarchaeology and food in the Maya area
sources.note: Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico / Estudios de Cultura Maya. Comparative context for animal foods and regional variation. Caution: Cross-region synthesis cannot substitute for a northern-Yucatan context.

sources.title: Zona arqueologica de Mayapan
sources.note: Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia (INAH). Accessible institutional baseline for the site's layout and chronology. Caution: Public summary; use specialized studies for contested chronology.

sources.title: Dental health in pre-Hispanic populations from Quintana Roo
sources.note: American Journal of Physical Anthropology / PubMed record. Supports cautious discussion of caries, tooth loss, diet, and oral health. Caution: Sample composition, place, and period must stay attached to findings.

sources.title: Social identity and dental modification at the Postclassic Maya urban centre of Mayapan
sources.note: Cambridge Archaeological Journal. Supports deliberate body modification as social/aesthetic practice. Caution: Do not call it primitive dentistry or assume universal participation.

sources.title: Fecal stanols reveal probable ancient Maya latrine pits at San Bartolo
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science. Rare direct evidence that certain pits probably served as latrines; also detects nixtamalization-related residues. Caution: About 700-800 years too early and outside Yucatan; cannot answer what a 1492 northern-Yucatan toilet was.

sources.title: Textiles and the Maya archaeological record
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Methodological basis for reconstructing perishable cloth from tools, impressions, imagery, and texts. Caution: Artifacts alone do not securely identify worker gender.

sources.title: Obsidian exchange on the east coast of the Yucatan Peninsula
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Material-sourcing evidence for long-distance exchange routes. Caution: Separate contexts and periods; obsidian movement does not itself define political control.

sources.title: Metalworking at Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico: discoveries from the R-183 group
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Context-rich evidence for metal production technology. Caution: Do not imply every town had metal workshops.

sources.title: Codice Maya de Mexico
sources.note: Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia (INAH). Authoritative portal for authenticity, materials, iconography, and early-Postclassic dating. Caution: Centuries too early for a 1492 sample and not securely localized to northern Yucatan.

sources.title: Late Postclassic lowland Maya politico-ritual architecture: temple assemblages and Zacpeten
sources.note: Ancient Mesoamerica. Comparative evidence for architecture linking political assembly and ritual. Caution: Not northern Yucatan; architectural parallels require explicit comparison label.

sources.title: Zona arqueologica de Tulum
sources.note: Instituto Nacional de Antropologia e Historia (INAH). Supports a fortified coastal center with maritime and ritual significance. Caution: Tulum is east-coast evidence, not a template for inland northern Yucatan.

sources.title: Mass violence and ritual desecration at Mayapan
sources.note: Journal of Anthropological Archaeology. Evidence for violent political breakdown and treatment of bodies/monuments. Caution: Sensational details need context and may predate the atlas window by decades.

sources.title: Maya literacy in colonial Yucatan, 1545-1580
sources.note: Estudios de Cultura Maya / UNAM. Supports adaptation of alphabetic Maya literacy in the decades after conquest. Caution: Latin-alphabet practice is later and transformed; do not show it as a 1492 writing sample.

proposedOverrides.summary: A modern atlas label for a politically diverse Maya region during an eight-year editorial interval.

batchIdentityNotes: Maya Yucateco is treated as a modern atlas label, not a single polity, ethnicity, border, or securely universal 1492 self-name.
The exact one-snapshot polygon extends south to Calakmul, Lamanai, and Tikal while excluding several northern and coastal probes.
The encoded Garifuna seam is explicitly identified as an anachronistic map artifact.
Direct archaeology, later colonial testimony, and modern comparison remain visibly separated.
No surviving northern-Yucatán text is securely dated to exactly 1492 to 1500; the writing sample is therefore explicitly unavailable.
The 1500 endpoint is a relabeling seam, not contact, conquest, collapse, or extinction.
